problem.title: Loan Stage Duration Analysis Function
problem.prompt: You are building a reporting tool for a lending platform. Write a PostgreSQL function named get_stage_durations that accepts two parameters: p_application_id (INTEGER) and p_min_hours (NUMERIC). The function should RETURNS TABLE(stage_name VARCHAR(100), entered_at TIMESTAMP, exited_at TIMESTAMP, duration_hours NUMERIC(10,2)). For the given application_id, return all stages the application passed through, calculating the time spent in each stage in hours (rounded to 2 decimals). Only include stages where duration_hours is greater than or equal to p_min_hours. Order results by entered_at ascending. If a stage has not been exited yet (exited_at IS NULL), exclude it from results. Your function must use RETURN QUERY with proper table aliasing to avoid column name conflicts.
problem.schema_ddl: CREATE TABLE loan_applications (application_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, borrower_name VARCHAR(200), requested_amount NUMERIC(12,2), submission_date DATE); CREATE TABLE application_stage_history (history_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, application_id INTEGER, stage_name VARCHAR(100), entered_at TIMESTAMP, exited_at TIMESTAMP);
problem.example_input_data: INSERT INTO loan_applications (application_id, borrower_name, requested_amount, submission_date) VALUES (1001, 'Alice Chen', 50000.00, '2024-01-10'), (1002, 'Bob Martinez', 75000.00, '2024-01-11'); INSERT INTO application_stage_history (history_id, application_id, stage_name, entered_at, exited_at) VALUES (1, 1001, 'Initial Review', '2024-01-10 09:00:00', '2024-01-10 11:30:00'), (2, 1001, 'Credit Check', '2024-01-10 11:30:00', '2024-01-10 12:00:00'), (3, 1001, 'Underwriting', '2024-01-10 12:00:00', '2024-01-11 14:00:00'), (4, 1001, 'Final Approval', '2024-01-11 14:00:00', '2024-01-11 15:00:00'), (5, 1002, 'Initial Review', '2024-01-11 08:00:00', '2024-01-11 09:00:00'), (6, 1002, 'Credit Check', '2024-01-11 09:00:00', NULL);

composite_moves: row-filter by exited_at IS NOT NULL

hints: Your function must accept two parameters and return a table with four columns matching the specified types exactly.
Use EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (exited_at - entered_at)) / 3600 to convert timestamp differences to hours, then round to 2 decimals.
Inside RETURN QUERY, alias the application_stage_history table and qualify every column reference (e.g., ash.stage_name) to prevent shadowing conflicts with the RETURNS TABLE column names.
problem.answer_key: CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION get_stage_durations(p_application_id INTEGER, p_min_hours NUMERIC) RETURNS TABLE(stage_name VARCHAR(100), entered_at TIMESTAMP, exited_at TIMESTAMP, duration_hours NUMERIC(10,2)) AS $$ BEGIN RETURN QUERY ( SELECT ash.stage_name, ash.entered_at, ash.exited_at, ROUND(CAST(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (ash.exited_at - ash.entered_at)) / 3600 AS NUMERIC), 2) AS duration_hours FROM application_stage_history ash WHERE ash.application_id = p_application_id AND ash.exited_at IS NOT NULL AND ROUND(CAST(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (ash.exited_at - ash.entered_at)) / 3600 AS NUMERIC), 2) >= p_min_hours ORDER BY ash.entered_at ); END; $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql; SELECT * FROM get_stage_durations(1001, 1.00);

_meta.scenario: a lending platform tracking loan application stages and approval times
